title: Medical Microbiology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L Medical Microbiology curriculum: normal microbial flora, mechanisms of bacterial pathogenicity and virulence factors, and the major medically important bacterial pathogens, their diseases, and basic laboratory diagnosis -- complements Immunology (host response) and Public Health Microbiology (population-level control) without repeating their content.

questions.question: The community of microorganisms that permanently and harmlessly colonises specific body sites such as the skin and gut in healthy individuals is called the:
questions.correct_answer: Normal (resident) flora
questions.explanation: Normal flora consists of microorganisms that consistently inhabit particular body sites without causing disease, and may even help exclude pathogens.

questions.question: An organism that is normally harmless but causes disease when host defenses are weakened or when it reaches an unusual body site is called a/an:
questions.correct_answer: Opportunistic pathogen
questions.explanation: Opportunistic pathogens, such as Candida albicans or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, exploit a weakened immune system, disrupted flora, or breach of normal barriers to cause infection.

questions.question: The ability of a microorganism to cause disease is termed:
questions.correct_answer: Pathogenicity
questions.explanation: Pathogenicity is the qualitative capacity of an organism to produce disease, while virulence refers to the quantitative degree or severity of pathogenicity.

questions.question: Bacterial structures or products that enhance a pathogen's ability to cause disease, such as capsules, toxins and adhesins, are collectively called:
questions.correct_answer: Virulence factors
questions.explanation: Virulence factors are molecules produced or expressed by pathogens that enable colonisation, immune evasion, invasion, or damage to host tissue.

questions.question: Bacterial exotoxins differ from endotoxins mainly in that exotoxins are:
options: Proteins actively secreted by living bacteria, often highly specific and potent
Lipopolysaccharide components released only on bacterial cell lysis
Non-antigenic and cannot be neutralised by antibodies
questions.correct_answer: Proteins actively secreted by living bacteria, often highly specific and potent
questions.explanation: Exotoxins are secreted proteins with specific modes of action (e.g., tetanus toxin blocking neurotransmitter release), whereas endotoxin (lipid A of LPS) is a structural component released mainly upon lysis of Gram-negative bacteria.

questions.question: The toxin responsible for the severe watery diarrhoea of cholera acts by:
options: Activating adenylate cyclase, causing excessive secretion of chloride ions and water into the intestinal lumen
Blocking acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions
Inhibiting protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylating elongation factor 2
questions.correct_answer: Activating adenylate cyclase, causing excessive secretion of chloride ions and water into the intestinal lumen
questions.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates a G-protein, locking adenylate cyclase in an active state; the resulting rise in cAMP drives massive chloride and water secretion, producing profuse watery ('rice-water') stools.

questions.question: Which bacterium is the causative agent of tuberculosis?
questions.correct_answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, an acid-fast bacillus with a waxy mycolic acid-rich cell wall, is the causative agent of tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs.

questions.question: The acid-fast staining property of Mycobacterium species is due to the high content of which cell wall component?
questions.correct_answer: Mycolic acid
questions.explanation: Mycolic acids are long-chain fatty acids in the mycobacterial cell wall that resist decolourisation with acid-alcohol after carbol fuchsin staining, the basis of the Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain.

questions.question: Staphylococcus aureus is typically differentiated from other staphylococci in the clinical laboratory by a positive result in the:
questions.correct_answer: Coagulase test
questions.explanation: S. aureus produces coagulase, an enzyme that clots plasma; a positive coagulase test distinguishes it from coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis.

questions.question: Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) is the causative agent of:
options: Streptococcal pharyngitis (strep throat) and scarlet fever
questions.correct_answer: Streptococcal pharyngitis (strep throat) and scarlet fever
questions.explanation: Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) causes pharyngitis, scarlet fever, impetigo, and, if untreated, can lead to rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis as post-streptococcal sequelae.

questions.question: On blood agar, complete lysis of red blood cells producing a clear zone around bacterial colonies is termed:
questions.correct_answer: Beta-haemolysis
questions.explanation: Beta-haemolysis is complete lysis of erythrocytes producing a clear zone, as seen with Streptococcus pyogenes; alpha-haemolysis produces partial, greenish lysis, and gamma-haemolysis indicates no lysis.

questions.question: Salmonella Typhi, the causative agent of typhoid fever, is primarily transmitted by:
options: The faecal-oral route via contaminated food or water
questions.correct_answer: The faecal-oral route via contaminated food or water
questions.explanation: Typhoid fever spreads mainly through ingestion of food or water contaminated with faeces from an infected person or carrier, reflecting Salmonella Typhi's enteric route of infection.

questions.question: A chronic, asymptomatic carrier who continues to shed Salmonella Typhi in stool long after recovering from typhoid fever, often colonised in the gallbladder, exemplifies:
questions.correct_answer: A carrier state of infection
questions.explanation: Some individuals, historically epitomised by 'Typhoid Mary', harbour S. Typhi in the gallbladder and continue shedding the organism without symptoms, posing an ongoing transmission risk.

questions.question: Escherichia coli O157:H7 is notable among E. coli strains for producing:
options: Shiga-like (verotoxin) toxin causing haemorrhagic colitis and haemolytic uraemic syndrome
questions.correct_answer: Shiga-like (verotoxin) toxin causing haemorrhagic colitis and haemolytic uraemic syndrome
questions.explanation: Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 produces Shiga-like toxins that damage intestinal and renal endothelium, causing bloody diarrhoea and, in severe cases, haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

questions.question: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is characteristically seen microscopically as:
options: Gram-negative diplococci, often intracellular within neutrophils
questions.correct_answer: Gram-negative diplococci, often intracellular within neutrophils
questions.explanation: N. gonorrhoeae appears as Gram-negative, kidney bean-shaped diplococci, classically seen inside neutrophils in Gram-stained urethral or cervical discharge smears, aiding rapid diagnosis.

questions.question: Clostridium tetani causes tetanus by producing a toxin that:
options: Blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters, causing sustained (spastic) muscle contraction
Blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis
Increases cAMP levels in intestinal cells
questions.correct_answer: Blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters, causing sustained (spastic) muscle contraction
questions.explanation: Tetanospasmin blocks release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA in the spinal cord, removing inhibition of motor neurons and causing sustained spastic muscle contractions (lockjaw).

questions.question: Clostridium botulinum causes botulism through a toxin that produces paralysis by:
options: Blocking the release of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions, causing flaccid paralysis
Blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release, causing spastic paralysis
questions.correct_answer: Blocking the release of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions, causing flaccid paralysis
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin prevents acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions, causing descending flaccid paralysis, in contrast to the spastic paralysis caused by tetanus toxin.

questions.question: Which organism is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in neonates, often acquired from the maternal genital tract during birth?
questions.correct_answer: Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae)
questions.explanation: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus) colonises the maternal vagina and is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis acquired during passage through the birth canal.

questions.question: A characteristic Gram-stain and morphology finding used to help identify Corynebacterium diphtheriae is:
options: Gram-positive, club-shaped rods arranged in 'Chinese letter' or palisade patterns
questions.correct_answer: Gram-positive, club-shaped rods arranged in 'Chinese letter' or palisade patterns
questions.explanation: C. diphtheriae is a Gram-positive, pleomorphic, club-shaped bacillus that characteristically arranges in angular clusters resembling Chinese letters or palisades on microscopy.

questions.question: Vibrio cholerae is morphologically described as a:
options: Gram-negative, comma-shaped rod with a single polar flagellum
questions.correct_answer: Gram-negative, comma-shaped rod with a single polar flagellum
questions.explanation: Vibrio cholerae is a curved, comma-shaped, Gram-negative bacillus that is highly motile due to a single polar flagellum, a feature used in its rapid darkfield microscopic identification.

questions.question: Helicobacter pylori, associated with peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, survives the acidic stomach environment mainly through production of the enzyme:
options: Urease, which hydrolyses urea to produce ammonia that neutralises local acid
Catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide
questions.correct_answer: Urease, which hydrolyses urea to produce ammonia that neutralises local acid
questions.explanation: H. pylori's urease converts urea to ammonia and carbon dioxide, creating a locally neutral microenvironment that protects the bacterium from gastric acidity; this is exploited in the urea breath test for diagnosis.

questions.question: The four basic diagnostic approaches used to confirm bacterial infections in a clinical laboratory include microscopy, culture, biochemical testing, and:
questions.correct_answer: Serology (antibody/antigen detection)
questions.explanation: Serological tests detect specific antibodies in patient serum or microbial antigens directly, complementing microscopy, culture and biochemical identification in confirming infection.

questions.question: The Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion method is used in the clinical laboratory to determine:
options: Antibiotic susceptibility of a bacterial isolate
The Gram reaction of a bacterium
The oxygen requirement of an organism
The optimum growth temperature of an organism
questions.correct_answer: Antibiotic susceptibility of a bacterial isolate
questions.explanation: In the Kirby-Bauer method, antibiotic-impregnated discs are placed on an agar plate seeded with the test organism, and the diameter of the resulting zone of inhibition indicates susceptibility or resistance.

questions.question: A hospital-acquired infection, defined as one that develops 48 hours or more after admission and was not present or incubating at the time of admission, is termed a/an:
questions.correct_answer: Nosocomial infection
questions.explanation: Nosocomial (healthcare-associated) infections are acquired during a hospital stay and were not present or incubating at admission, and are often caused by resistant organisms such as MRSA.

questions.question: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) achieves resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics mainly by:
options: Producing an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for beta-lactams
questions.correct_answer: Producing an altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) with low affinity for beta-lactams
questions.explanation: MRSA carries the mecA gene encoding PBP2a, a modified penicillin-binding protein with markedly reduced affinity for beta-lactam antibiotics, conferring broad resistance to this drug class.

questions.question: Antibiotics that inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit include:
questions.correct_answer: Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides (e.g., streptomycin) and tetracyclines target the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, exploiting the difference between 70S prokaryotic and 80S eukaryotic ribosomes for selective toxicity.

questions.question: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin act by inhibiting:
questions.correct_answer: DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II)
questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, enzymes essential for DNA supercoiling and replication, causing lethal DNA damage.

questions.question: The primary mode of transmission for Mycobacterium tuberculosis is:
options: Airborne droplet nuclei from coughing or sneezing
questions.correct_answer: Airborne droplet nuclei from coughing or sneezing
questions.explanation: M. tuberculosis is spread mainly through inhalation of small airborne droplet nuclei expelled when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or speaks.

questions.question: Bacillus anthracis, the causative agent of anthrax, is distinguished among Gram-positive rods by its:
options: Ability to form highly resistant endospores and its antiphagocytic capsule of poly-D-glutamic acid
Complete lack of a cell wall
Requirement for a living host cell to replicate
questions.correct_answer: Ability to form highly resistant endospores and its antiphagocytic capsule of poly-D-glutamic acid
questions.explanation: B. anthracis forms extremely resistant endospores that can persist in soil for decades, and its unusual polypeptide capsule helps the vegetative form evade phagocytosis during infection.

questions.question: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a notable opportunistic pathogen in hospitals mainly because it:
options: Is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics and thrives in moist hospital environments
Only infects healthy individuals with strong immune systems
questions.correct_answer: Is intrinsically resistant to many antibiotics and thrives in moist hospital environments
questions.explanation: P. aeruginosa has intrinsic resistance to numerous antibiotics and can survive in moist environments such as sinks, catheters and ventilator equipment, making it a common cause of nosocomial infection in immunocompromised patients.

questions.question: The oxidase test, used to help identify Neisseria and Pseudomonas species, detects the presence of:
options: Cytochrome c oxidase, part of the electron transport chain
questions.correct_answer: Cytochrome c oxidase, part of the electron transport chain
questions.explanation: The oxidase test detects bacterial cytochrome c oxidase, which oxidises a redox indicator to a coloured product; a positive result helps distinguish oxidase-positive organisms like Neisseria and Pseudomonas from oxidase-negative Enterobacteriaceae.

questions.question: The triple sugar iron (TSI) agar test in diagnostic bacteriology is primarily used to assess an organism's ability to:
options: Ferment glucose, lactose and sucrose, and to produce hydrogen sulfide gas
questions.correct_answer: Ferment glucose, lactose and sucrose, and to produce hydrogen sulfide gas
questions.explanation: TSI agar reveals sugar fermentation patterns (via colour changes in the slant and butt), gas production, and hydrogen sulfide production (blackening), helping differentiate members of the Enterobacteriaceae.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a superinfection?
options: A new infection that arises when antibiotic therapy disrupts normal flora, allowing resistant or opportunistic organisms to overgrow
An infection acquired before hospital admission
An infection caused by a virus rather than a bacterium
questions.correct_answer: A new infection that arises when antibiotic therapy disrupts normal flora, allowing resistant or opportunistic organisms to overgrow
questions.explanation: Broad-spectrum antibiotic use can eliminate protective normal flora, creating an ecological niche in which resistant bacteria or fungi (e.g., Clostridioides difficile, Candida) overgrow and cause a superinfection.
